source.title: No Data Augmentation? Alternative Regularizations for Effective Training on Small Datasets

record.file_problem: Text contains the complete paper, including experiments and conclusions.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own model-width, training-length, and parameter-norm results relevant to generalization, using a small natural-label dataset and test accuracy/loss rather than the claim versions' exact setups.
record.gate_note: The paper studies CIFAR-10 small-data training with 50 examples per class, testing on ciFAIR-10. It does not use random labels or measure training-test error gaps directly. Its own results on momentum, width, training length, and parameter norm are included; cited prior-work claims and state-of-the-art comparisons are not extracted as results of this study. Values in Figures 5 and 7 are figure-only where no exact values are stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The width experiments bear on V2 in a new setting: small-data WRNs whose model-selection procedure filters for 100% training accuracy. Wider networks improve held-out accuracy despite the smallest architecture already fitting the training set. Weight decay, augmentation and fixed training schedules distinguish this from V2's original unregularized, convergence-trained setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute improved small-data classification to hyperparameter selection, model widening and longer training, reporting 66.5% for the selected WRN-16-22. The highest-scoring configuration reaches 67.6%, so 66.5% should not be described as the grid maximum.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses WRNs on CIFAR-10 with only 50 examples per class, basic flips and translations, and ciFAIR-10 testing; it does not test the original claim's random-label, optimizer-comparison, dropout, or sharpness setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Test performance varies with learning rate and weight decay, momentum condition, model width, training length, and selection using a small validation set versus the parameter-norm heuristic.

fits_no_version.finding: Smaller parameter norms after 50 steps predict lower test loss among models reaching 100% training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early parameter norm predicts held-out loss within the tested WRN configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Norm-based hyperparameter selection and subsequent momentum removal improve selected WRN-16-1 accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed selection and training recipe improves small-data classification over the validation-selected baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD with and without momentum achieves similar test losses across matched hyperparameter comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Momentum provides no clear held-out advantage in this small-data WRN setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing training from 25k to 75k steps improves maximum accuracy at every tested width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longer training improves small-data WRN accuracy with batch size fixed at 10.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger learning-rate–weight-decay products produce faster norm decay, noisier accuracy trajectories and better generalization among fitted models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These training-dynamics features accompany better test performance in the tested WRN-16-10 configurations.

record.peer_reviewed: 2023 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops (ICCVW)
record.problems: The experiments cover a single small-data image-classification benchmark, with batch size fixed at 10 and minimal augmentation. The study does not measure training-test gaps directly. Figure 4 summarizes momentum comparisons as pairwise proportions without uncertainty estimates. Some width-sweep values appear only in figures, and the figure transcription is flattened.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible experimental results were left out. The state-of-the-art comparison in Table 1 is not extracted as a result for the claim versions, and cited results from other papers are excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the natural-versus-random-label held-out comparison.
The interpolation threshold, training to convergence, and widening without explicit regularization. The experiments use weight decay, basic augmentation and fixed training schedules.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons and recovery of a large-batch penalty; batch size remains 10.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Memorization-based example removal versus random removal.

missing.what: Width gains depend on hyperparameter tuning: with weight decay fixed at 5×10^-5, widening from 1 to 22 improves maximum accuracy by approximately three points; searching weight decay as well raises the gain to approximately seven points. This condition should accompany R6's width result.
missing.locator: Section 4.7, Importance of HPs selection; Figure 6

record.verdict_notes: V2 receives qualified evidence in a regularized convolutional setting, not a replication of its original recipe. Neither natural-label fitting alone nor the parameter-norm analysis establishes V1 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization experiment or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out performance.

No width sweep beyond interpolation with the stated one-hidden-layer ReLU architectures; networks are WRNs, and zero training error is not used to test how test error changes past an interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures or local connectivity.
No large-batch comparison; batch size is fixed at 10.
The study relates parameter norm to test loss, but does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare its ranking against norm- and margin-based generalization measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: WRN-16-1
rows.operation_detail: Removed momentum while selecting hyperparameters using the parameter-norm heuristic

conditions.value: ciFAIR-10 test set; 1% CIFAR-10 training set

rows.baseline: 53.3% baseline WRN-16-1 selected using small validation set
rows.note: The text attributes the gain to both removing momentum and selecting hyperparameters with the new metric; it does not isolate either intervention's effect.
rows.check: This is the authors' training and selection method comparison, not a listed claim test. The intermediate baseline is 56.9% with norm-based selection and momentum; removing momentum raises the selected result to 58.1%. The 53.3% baseline combines both changes.

rows.note: The paper states about 50% of the time the best models are either with µ = 0.0 or µ = 0.9, indicating similar test performance.
rows.check: SGD with versus without momentum does not test the adaptive-versus-SGD comparison in V4. Similar performance is reported, but 'absent' is not a state for any linked version.

rows.subject: WRN-16-1, WRN-16-3, WRN-16-10, WRN-16-22
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximum test accuracy across model widths and training lengths

conditions.value: ciFAIR-10 test set; 1% CIFAR-10 training set

rows.measure: Maximum test accuracy by width and training length
rows.value: Figure 5 shows higher maximum test accuracy at 75k iterations for each width; text reports gains of 4, 1.5, 1.6, and 2.1 percentage points for widths 1, 3, 10, and 22, respectively.
rows.note: The paper reports improvements at all four model widths.
rows.check: Longer training at a fixed batch size does not test V5's batch-size penalty or its recovery. The reported training-length gains are valid but outside the listed versions.

rows.subject: WRN-16-1, WRN-16-3, WRN-16-10, WRN-16-22
rows.operation_detail: Increased width and compared maximum test accuracy

conditions.value: ciFAIR-10 test set; 1% CIFAR-10 training set

rows.baseline: WRN-16-1; exact value not stated in the Section 4.4 width comparison
rows.value: WRN-16-3: 62.8%; WRN-16-10: 65.2%; WRN-16-22: figure-only in Figure 6
rows.note: Section 4.4 states 3× width gives a 4.4 percentage-point increase, and reports maximum accuracy 62.8% for width 3 and 65.2% for width 10. Width-22 grid values are not fully recoverable from the flattened figure transcription.
rows.check: The width sweep bears on V2 because the smallest architecture can already fit the training set. Separate the clear improvement through width 10 from the plateau at width 22. Figure 6 gives maximum accuracies of 58.4%, 62.8%, 65.2% and 65.5% for widths 1, 3, 10 and 22. The selected width-1 model's 58.1% is not the grid maximum.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 4 and 4.4; Figure 6 and caption. Section 4.4 states 62.8% and 65.2%; Figure 6 includes 58.4% and 65.5%.

rows.subject: WRN-16-10
rows.operation_detail: Tracked parameter norm and test accuracy over training for models reaching 100% training accuracy

conditions.value: ciFAIR-10 test set; 1% CIFAR-10 training set

rows.measure: Test accuracy and parameter norm over epochs
rows.value: Figure 7 shows that larger αλ combinations that fit the training set have faster parameter-norm decay and noisier test-accuracy profiles; the authors state they generalize better.
rows.note: Exact accuracy values are not stated in the prose. This is an association, not a direct measurement of the train-test gap.
rows.check: Norm decay and noisy test-accuracy trajectories do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps.
